2._section_summary: This abstract describes a study involving 143 undergraduate women who completed self-reports on exercise behavior, body orientation, body appreciation, and body-related talk. The results indicated that conversations about exercise and weight loss/dieting differentially predicted body appreciation. Specifically, the relationship between talk type and body appreciation was explained by the object–process dichotomy, with exercise conversations predicting body appreciation through considering what bodies can do, and weight loss/dieting conversations being mediated by negative body attitudes.

The study found that exercise talk predicted increased body appreciation, while weight loss/dieting talk predicted decreased appreciation, with these relationships mediated by object-process attitudes and orientation. The sample consisted of undergraduate women, and limitations regarding generalizability, measures (including the BES scale for body orientation), and causal direction were discussed.

9._section_summary: This section presents descriptive statistics and bivariate correlations among various measures related to body appreciation, body orientation (appearance vs. performance, body-as-process vs. body-as-object), and body-related talk. It highlights that participants were more oriented toward appearance than performance, and women's attitudes toward body-as-process were more positive than body-as-object. Correlations, referenced in Table 1 (not provided), indicate that exercise was positively related to body appreciation and process orientation, while negatively associated with object orientation. Conversations about exercise were positively associated with body appreciation, whereas conversations about weight loss and dieting were negatively associated with it. The section describes findings from a single study, referred to as Study X.

10._section_summary: This section details a simultaneous multiple regression analysis conducted to examine how weight loss talk and exercise talk predict body appreciation, while controlling for BMI. The analysis involved 138 participants. The overall model was significant, and results indicated that increased BMI and increased weight loss talk were associated with less body appreciation, whereas increased exercise talk predicted more body appreciation. The study is referred to as 'Study X' as no specific study number was provided.

11._section_summary: This section details mediation analyses conducted to examine how body esteem and body orientations mediate the relationship between body-related talk (exercise talk, weight loss talk) and body appreciation. The results, based on 5000 bootstrapped samples and presented across Figure 1(a) to 1(d), indicate varying degrees of mediation. For instance, body esteem fully mediated the relationship between exercise talk and body appreciation, while only performance orientation mediated this relationship in another model. For weight-loss/diet talk, attitudes toward appearance partially mediated the relationship, but neither performance nor appearance orientation mediated it in a separate analysis. The text describes a single set of analyses without explicitly naming a study.

14._extracted_caption: Figure 1. Attitudes and orientations as mediators in the relationship between body-related talk and body appreciation. (a) Attitudes as mediators for exercise talk and body appreciation, F(3, 138) = 53.66, p < .001, r2 = .54. (b) Orientations as mediators for exercise talk and body appreciation, F(3, 137) = 14.40, p < .001, r2 = .24. (c) Attitudes as mediators for weight-loss talk and body appreciation, F(3, 138) = 62.14, p < .001, r2 = .57. (d) Orientations as mediators for weight-loss talk and body appreciation, F(3, 137) = 22.23, p < .001, r2 = .33. Unstandardized path coefficients are presented. The coefficients in parentheses represent the direct relationship between body-related talk and body appreciation.
